## Why this page exists

This session is remote (async). There is no lecture to sit through — instead, there is a debrief, a standard to learn, and a personal document for you to write and keep.

By now (S4–S10) you have used an agent to write code, wrangle data, run models, and generate output, in both R and Python. At least once, the agent almost certainly produced something that *looked* right and *was not*. That is not a hypothetical: it is the single most reliable thing about working with LLMs, and it is the reason this course spends two full sessions (S7, S8) on testing before circling back to it here.

This page connects two things that are usually taught separately:

1. **What a professional reproducibility standard actually demands** — the lens I use as Data Editor of the *Journal of Political Economy* when I check whether an accepted paper's results can be regenerated from its code and data.
2. **What you have personally already seen go wrong** in this course, and what caught it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Objectives
- Understand what a journal-grade replication package requires, and why each requirement exists.
- Catalogue every case in S4–S10 where an agent produced a plausible-but-wrong result, and identify what caught it.
- Write a personal checklist you will actually use the next time an agent writes code for you.
:::

## Part 1 — The Data Editor's lens

When a paper is conditionally accepted at a journal like the *JPE*, the authors submit a **replication package**: code, data (or a data-availability statement explaining why not), and documentation, sufficient for someone who was not involved in the project to regenerate every table and figure in the paper. My job as Data Editor is to check whether that is actually true — not whether the authors *say* it's true.

The standard is not exotic. It is a small number of concrete requirements, each of which maps onto a failure mode you have already lived through in this course:

| Requirement | What it actually checks | Failure mode it prevents |
|---|---|---|
| **One-command (or documented multi-step) run** | Someone other than the author can regenerate output without private knowledge of "the trick" | Code that only runs on the author's machine because of an undocumented step |
| **Pinned software/package versions** | Results don't silently change because a dependency updated | "Worked yesterday" — a package update changes default behavior |
| **No hardcoded absolute paths** | Code runs on any machine, not just the author's | `/Users/yourname/Desktop/data.csv` breaks for everyone else (this is exactly what S3 required of your own repo) |
| **Data provenance documented** | Every input file's origin and any transformation is traceable | Silent, undocumented filtering or recoding upstream of the analysis |
| **README describing the mapping from code to output** | A stranger can find which script produces Table 3 | Output that "exists" somewhere but nobody, including the author six months later, can find how it was made |
| **Seeds set for anything stochastic** | Simulations, bootstraps, ML training are exactly reproducible | "Approximately the same" results that quietly drift each run |
| **Sample construction is auditable** | Every row-drop and filter is visible and justified | Silent sample-selection decisions that change the answer |

Notice what this standard is really about: it does not ask "is the code good style" or "is the paper's argument correct." It asks **can this specific, exact result be regenerated by someone who is not you, using only what you gave them.** That is a narrower and more mechanical question than "is this correct" — and it is exactly the right question to ask about anything an agent wrote, because an agent will happily hand you code that runs, produces a plausible number, and is *only correct by accident, once, on your machine, with your data*.

This is also why S3 made you restructure your repo (paths, README, config) before you had a "publication" to worry about: reproducibility discipline is infrastructure you build in from session one, not a checklist you apply retroactively to a finished project.

## Part 2 — Debrief: the failure log

Across S4–S10 you used agents for: writing small scripts (S2), building a DuckDB pipeline (S6), writing unit tests against that pipeline (S7), and writing invariant/property-based checks and hunting a seeded bug (S8), spatial joins and CRS transforms (S10), and reasoning about cost/scale tradeoffs (S9). S4 gave you the underlying reason all of this happens: hallucination is a structural property of how an LLM generates text, not an occasional glitch.

**Task.** Go back through your own work from S4–S10 (your repo history, your notes, your memory of "wait, that number looks wrong") and fill in this table with **at least four real entries** — not hypothetical ones. If you genuinely cannot find four, that is itself informative: it usually means you weren't checking closely enough, and you should look again, harder, before concluding the agent was flawless four sessions running.

| Session | What the agent produced | Why it was plausible | What actually caught it | Could a S7/S8-style test have caught it automatically? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| e.g. S6 | A join that silently dropped unmatched rows | Query ran without error, row count looked "reasonable" | Manually checked row count before vs. after join | Yes — a row-count invariant check |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |

For each row, be specific about the **mechanism**: was it a hallucinated number (S4: the model predicted a plausible-sounding token, not a looked-up fact)? A silent unit/CRS mismatch (S10: the map "looked fine" at first glance)? A test that passed but tested the wrong thing (S7/S8: arrange-act-assert on the wrong assertion)? A cost/scale estimate that assumed the wrong pricing tier (S9)? Naming the mechanism is what turns this from a diary into a diagnostic tool — it's the difference between "the agent was wrong" and "the agent was wrong *in this particular, recognizable way*."

If you cross-reference against your S7/S8 test suite: does a test already exist that would have caught this case? If not, is it worth adding one? You do not have to add it now, but note whether it's the kind of thing a test *could* catch (an invariant, a golden-output comparison, a row-count check) versus the kind of thing that fundamentally requires a human to look at output and judge whether it's sensible (a spatial join that "looks like a map" but uses the wrong projection — S10's example of a silent bug that survives casual inspection).

## Part 3 — Your personal checklist

This is the graded outcome of the session. Using Part 1 (the standard) and Part 2 (your own evidence of where things actually went wrong), write a **personal checklist** — a short document, in your own words, that you will genuinely use the next time an agent writes code for a project that matters to you.

It should not be a copy of the table in Part 1. It should be shorter, specific to *your* recurring failure patterns, and phrased as things you will actually do, not things one should generally do. A good checklist has maybe 6–10 items. Some prompts to get you started (do not just answer these one-for-one — synthesize):

- Which of your Part 2 entries would you have caught *immediately* if you had just followed one habit? Put that habit at the top.
- Is there a category of check (row counts, unit tests, CRS/units sanity checks, seed-setting, path hardcoding) that shows up more than once in your table? That is a signal, not a coincidence.
- What's the cheapest check you can run every time, versus the expensive check you'll only run before something ships (a presentation, a submission, handing code to a collaborator)?
- Given S9 (cost/model economics): is there a point where "run every check every time" becomes wasteful, and how do you decide?
- If a reviewer (or a Data Editor) picked up your S12 capstone repo cold, what from Part 1's table would already be satisfied by your habits, and what would still be missing?

::: {.callout-note}
## Deliverable
A short written checklist (this can live at the top of your S12 capstone README, or as a standalone note in your course repo). Bring it to S12 — you will use it.
:::
